# Single cells and tissue space

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/08-singlecell-spatial.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader.
:::

A bulk measurement of isoform usage averages over every cell in the sample. If
two cell types each use one isoform exclusively, and the sample holds equal
numbers of both, the bulk answer is a fifty-fifty mixture that no cell produces.
Single-cell and spatial methods exist to break that average open. The list of
questions they have actually settled is narrower.

## CD45 splice forms mark T cell subsets {#sec-ptprc}

@sec-cd45 treated CD45 as a receptor whose splice choice tunes signalling. In
single-cell data the same gene works as a subset marker, and gene-level
counting cannot read it.

In human CD8 T cells profiled with a 5' assay, naive and
effector-memory-reexpressing-CD45RA clusters carried the CD45RA form of PTPRC,
while central memory and MAIT cells carried CD45RO
[@michalik2024ideis]. The gene is expressed in all of them, and only the splice
form distinguishes them.

Mouse leukocytes behave the same way, with Cd45RB marking naive and central
memory T cells plus NK cells, and Cd45RC essentially unused
[@michalik2024ideis].

## Whether splicing finds new cell populations {#sec-sc-structure}

Splice-isoform quantification split human blood classical monocytes into two
subpopulations that gene-expression clustering of the same cells did not
resolve [@olivieri2021splicing].

Splicing also carries enough information to place a cell. Unsupervised
clustering on the splicing scores of just two ubiquitously expressed genes
assigned individual human cells to the right tissue compartment. Accuracy was
78, 84 and 95 per cent for stromal, epithelial and immune cells in one donor. In
a second donor with a third as many cells it was 70, 100 and 49 per cent
[@olivieri2021splicing].

The counterweight is from a different group and should be read alongside. An
annotation-free analysis of two large mouse single-cell atlases found splicing
strongly tied to cell identity. In those authors' hands it never revealed a cell
subpopulation that expression clustering had missed [@benegas2022robust].
Whether isoform data finds new populations or only describes known ones is not
settled.

## Isoform change without gene change {#sec-isoform-only}

The fraction of isoform differences invisible to gene-level analysis has been
measured in single cells as it was in tumours.

Across a cross-tissue single-cell long-read atlas, a third of the cases where
isoform proportions differed between cell classes showed no significant change
in the gene's total expression [@mantri2026splice].

A mouse and human brain isoform map covering roughly 200,000 cells put it
higher. About seven in ten genes carry isoforms whose variation across
development, region or subtype is not explained by variation in the gene's own
expression [@joglekar2024singlecell].

A single-cell long-read atlas of human CD8 T cells found that about half the
isoforms differing between cells of one cluster sat in genes whose totals
differed as well. Those authors read the remainder as isoform-specific
regulation [@tzaban2025rna].

Cell type matters more than tissue for one of those two quantities, and the two
contribute comparably for the other. How widely a gene spreads its expression
across isoforms tracked cell type more strongly than tissue of residence, at
mean partial omega-squared 0.062 against 0.047. Which isoforms a gene used
contributed comparably from cell type and from tissue, once factor complexity
was accounted for [@mantri2026splice].

## Brain cell types at isoform resolution {#sec-brain-atlas}

Single cells let a regional difference be charged to a compartment. In postnatal
mouse hippocampus against prefrontal cortex, three quarters of the isoform
differences visible in pooled tissue could be charged to one compartment alone,
neuronal or non-neuronal, rather than to a coordinated change in both
[@joglekar2021spatially].

Sometimes the annotated cell type is the thing that breaks. For a developmental
gene with a neuron-specific isoform, part of a granule neuroblast population
used the excitatory-neuron isoform and the rest used the non-neuronal one. Those
authors suggest the neuroblasts may not be one population
[@joglekar2021spatially].

The programmes transfer between species, and exons that distinguished mouse
brain cell types tended to distinguish the same cell types in human hippocampus
[@joglekar2024singlecell].

## Immune subsets at isoform resolution {#sec-sc-methods}

Long-read profiling of 29 sorted human immune subsets found one receptor gene
using different isoforms in two T cell states. A Th17-restricted IL23R form sat
alongside a separate form restricted to activated regulatory T cells
[@inamo2024trails]. The receptor is the same gene in both states and a
different molecule.

## Isoforms sorted between soma and dendrite {#sec-localisation}

Isoform identity predicts location inside a neuron. Sequencing soma and
dendrite separately from the same single mouse neurons found 2,225
dendritically localised RNAs. In 298 of those cases one 3' UTR isoform of a
gene localised and another did not [@middleton2019comprehensive].

The difference starts at the transcript rather than at the protein. For a small
GTPase that shapes neuronal morphology, the two last-exon isoforms separated
between the neurite and the cell body as mRNA [@ciollimattioli2018alternative].

## Three-prime ends across cell types {#sec-sc-apa}

Poly(A) site choice is the isoform axis that ordinary single-cell chemistry
measures best, because most protocols read the 3' end.

Across roughly two million nuclei spanning five stages of mouse embryonic
development, 3' UTRs lengthened globally in every cell type examined. Within
each stage, blood lineages sat at the short end and neuronal cell types at the
long end [@agarwal2021landscape].

The scale is large and the overlap with expression is small. Analysing 474
human and mouse cell types, the dominant 3' UTR isoform switches in 60 per cent
of human genes in at least one cell type. Only about a tenth of differential 3'
UTR events coincide with a change in that gene's expression
[@fansler2024quantifying]. Length and abundance are two outputs of the same
gene.

The signal is recoverable from data collected for other purposes. Mining
ordinary 3'-tag single-cell data from mouse T cells recovered 868
polyadenylation shifts between resting and activated cells, skewed toward
shorter 3' UTRs in the dividing population [@shulman2019celltype]. In the Fly
Cell Atlas nuclei, some genes resolved their 3' isoform choice reliably in
single cells rather than only in pooled clusters, and this worked best in
neurons [@lee2022diverse].

## Does one cell use one isoform or several {#sec-bimodality}

The literature has moved twice on this one, and it is still open.

![Three illustrative populations of cells, each with the same population mean.
A bulk assay returns one number for all three, which is why the question had to
be asked in single cells.](../figures/within-cell-isoform.svg){#fig-within-cell width=100%}

The early evidence pointed at real cell-to-cell choice. Single-cell
polyadenylation-site mapping was applied to genetically and developmentally
uniform stem cell populations. It found cell-to-cell differences in 3' end
preference larger than technical noise and random molecule partitioning together
could produce [@velten2015single]. Single-molecule imaging of one gene showed
that an individual active transcription site in the nucleus is dominated by one
3' isoform. Those authors offer that as a hint that a polyadenylation site, once
chosen, stays active for several rounds of transcription [@velten2015single].

Then the all-or-nothing picture was attacked at its root. A reanalysis of human
and mouse single-cell datasets, together with a probabilistic model, argued that
the apparently all-or-nothing splicing of single cells is a technical artefact.
Biology accounts for almost none of it on that reading
[@buenabadnajar2020coverage]. A later review records that the bimodal picture
survives for only about a fifth of exons once subsequent studies looked, with
single-peaked distributions the commoner outcome [@joglekar2023words].

The current position leans toward mixtures within cells. Modelling isoform
heterogeneity
within cells against between cells, across single-cell and spatial long-read
datasets, one group concluded that individual cells routinely carry more than
one isoform of a well-expressed gene [@fu2025longcell].

The same group reports the opposite behaviour in one spatial dataset. In Visium
data from a mouse olfactory bulb slice, each cell within a layer used one or
the other of a gene's two isoforms exclusively, and which one bore no relation
to the layer [@fu2025longcell]. That measurement is per spot rather than per
cell, and an apparently sharp choice with no spatial pattern is hard to read as
a programme.

## Isoform use mapped in tissue sections {#sec-spatial}

Spatial methods give an orthogonal check on single-cell isoform calls. Long-read
sequencing of a spatially barcoded brain section reproduced the direction of
the single-cell regional splicing difference for 85 per cent of 40
region-specific exons [@joglekar2021spatially].

Imaging adds cases a gene-level map cannot represent at all.
Isoform-resolved imaging of mouse brain sections caught one
transcription-factor gene producing a coding and a non-coding isoform that
occupied different places in the tissue and different cell types
[@cohen2025whole].

The load is unevenly distributed across the brain. Of roughly 1,400 genes with
spatially dependent isoform use, about 800 had a module tied to a hippocampal
subfield and about 100 to the choroid plexus [@cohen2025whole].

How many genes are called spatially variable depends heavily on the statistical
model. Reanalysing two published long-read spatial brain sections with a model
built for sparse isoform counts more than doubled the number called, from 61 to
150 reproducible across replicates [@su2025splisosm]. The same framework was
then applied to ordinary short-read spatial data from adult mouse brain. Over
eight hundred genes varied spatially in which 3' end they used, more than five
times the count recovered from long-read spatial data of the same tissue
[@su2025splisosm], so the cheaper assay returned more.

## Limits from cell number and testing {#sec-sc-limits}

A simulation study that modelled dropout and quantification error explicitly
concluded that resolving which isoforms an individual cell expresses is not
currently advisable with short-read single-cell RNA-seq
[@westoby2020obstacles]. That is the baseline against which everything above
should be read.

Which chemistry was used decides how much is reachable at all, and
@sec-sc-chemistry gives that comparison.

For rare cell types the binding constraint is cell number rather than depth. One
deep combinatorial-indexing experiment ran at fifty thousand reads per cell. An
abundant airway cell type of about fifteen thousand cells recovered 158,786 of
the junctions seen in matched bulk. The rarest type, of 68 cells, recovered
25,879 [@saferali2026framework]. Sequencing those 68 cells harder would not
have closed the gap.

The obvious design runs into a multiple-testing wall. Testing exon by exon on
single-cell long-read data from two mouse brain regions, only 31 of 2,132
testable genes,
1.45 per cent, survived a correction for dependent tests. Those authors
replaced the exon test with a single per-gene isoform test
[@joglekar2021spatially].

Breaking the bulk average open is now routine. Deciding what a single cell is
doing with a single gene remains hard, and most of the disagreements in this
chapter are about that second question.
